comparison: Both support the patient cohort and demographic claims (C1, C66, C103). OpenEval focuses on internal consistency of demographic data, while peer reviewers praised the 'incredibly rare dataset' and overall methodology quality.

Both support neuronal recording methodology (C2-C7). OpenEval validates specific counts and exclusion criteria, while peer reviewers praised 'careful, high quality methodology' including spike recording and sorting.

Both support technical recording setup claims (C67-C71). OpenEval validates equipment specifications and sampling rates, while peer reviewers endorsed the overall recording methodology as high quality.

Both support experimental design parameters (C72-C74, C104-C107). OpenEval validates timing and trial structure consistency, while peer reviewers praised the 'rigorous task design' and 'cleverly designed' experiment.

Both support spike sorting methodology (C75-C77). OpenEval validates standard methods with appropriate citations, while peer reviewers praised spike sorting as part of the 'careful, high quality methodology.'

Both support stimulation parameters (C78-C81, C107-C108). OpenEval notes internal consistency but mentions entrainment was not directly measured, while peer reviewers accepted the stimulation approach without critique.

Both support primary finding of neuronal modulation (C18-C20). OpenEval validates statistical testing but questions one-sided test choice, while peer reviewers emphasized this as 'an important demonstration' of stimulation effects.

Both support region-specific findings (C21-C24). OpenEval raises concern about multiple comparison correction with p-values near 0.05, while peer reviewers accepted regional selectivity findings without critique, noting 'neurons in all these areas were modulated...except the ACC.'

Both support low overlap between conditions (C25-C27). OpenEval notes the interpretation assumes independence of mechanisms, while peer reviewers praised the 'cleverly designed' experiment that 'teases apart responses' and accepted the distinct populations interpretation.

Divergent evaluations of rhythmicity finding (C28). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to analysis limited to 34.5% of units with firing rates ≥1 Hz, questioning generalizability. Peer reviewers SUPPORTED without concern, treating it as part of comprehensive analysis.

Both support baseline firing rate predictions (C29-C32). OpenEval validates non-parametric statistics and finding, while peer reviewers acknowledged the relationship and discussed modulation index choice in context of firing rates.

Divergent evaluations of parameter variation findings (C33-C34). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to very small sample sizes (n=30, n=1, n=6) making null results uninformative. Peer reviewers SUPPORTED, noting low-amplitude effects without questioning statistical power.

Both support temporal and directional modulation patterns (C35-C40). OpenEval notes mechanisms are unexplained, while peer reviewers praised the 'detailed and deep investigation' providing 'high confidence in validity.'

Both support effect size measurements (C41-C42). OpenEval notes lack of statistical comparison and unclear biological significance, while peer reviewers accepted as part of comprehensive characterization without specific critique.

Both support cell-type classification (C43-C49). OpenEval notes equal modulation claim lacks statistical testing and may be underpowered (n=23 inhibitory), while peer reviewers accepted methodology as part of 'careful, high quality' approach without concern.

Both support null behavioral findings (C50-C53). OpenEval notes contradiction with prior work (Inman et al., 2018) and questions experimental differences, while peer reviewers accepted as 'complementing' the 2018 paper without viewing as problematic.

Both support lack of neural-behavioral correlation (C54-C57). OpenEval notes threshold choice (±0.5) is somewhat arbitrary despite Cohen's d justification, while peer reviewers accepted as valid result rather than limitation.

Both support anatomical distance analysis (C58-C60). OpenEval notes limited range may have precluded effect detection, while peer reviewers accepted as part of comprehensive control analyses without concern.

Both support population-level PCA analyses (C61-C62). OpenEval notes analysis is qualitative without statistical testing and unclear biological interpretation, while peer reviewers praised as 'very useful resource' for the field.

Both support summary of heterogeneity and key findings (C63-C65). OpenEval validates statistical support for predictive factors, while peer reviewers accepted characterization as providing useful resource for brain stimulation research.

Both support analytical approaches (C109-C115). OpenEval validates methods as standard and appropriate with informal d-prime justification, while peer reviewers praised 'careful, high quality...statistical analysis.'

Both support background context claims (C8-C10, C82). OpenEval notes citations should be verified for specific claims, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted scientific rationale without questioning literature.

Both support prior work motivation (C11-C16). OpenEval notes C12 involves mechanistic inference that may not be directly demonstrated, while peer reviewers accepted framework as building appropriately on prior work.
Both support knowledge gap identification (C17). OpenEval notes some relevant animal studies exist, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted rationale as part of overall scientific framework.

Both support cell-type classification literature (C83-C86). OpenEval validates citations and consistency with established approaches, while peer reviewers accepted without specific comment as part of overall methodology.

Both support animal literature summary (C87-C91). OpenEval notes C91 involves speculation about mechanism that should be distinguished from demonstrated effects, while peer reviewers accepted background without critique.
Both support recent relevant work citations (C92-C95). OpenEval validates appropriateness for interpreting findings, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted as part of scientific framework.

Both support diverse prior stimulation work (C96-C101). OpenEval validates citations provide important context for heterogeneous responses, while peer reviewers accepted background literature without specific comment.

Both support contextualization of null behavioral finding (C102). OpenEval questions why study design didn't account for known variability sources, while peer reviewers accepted as appropriate contextualization without concern.
